newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Ringgit holds ground but remains vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ringgit holds ground but remains vulnerable.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit took a breather on Wednesday after a recent battering, but the worst was not over, foreign exchange dealers and analysts said.
They said pressure on the ringgit eased for now as the focus shifted to the Indonesian rupiah.
The rupiah tumbled to a historic low of 2,682 to the U.S. dollar earlier on Wednesday, before recovering to last trade at 2,660.

The slide in the rupiah was due to the contagion effect of weaker regional currencies and to an Indonesian newspaper report quoting an economist as saying Bank Indonesia should allow the currency to find its own level.
The ringgit was quoted around 2.7760 per dollar at 1144 GMT.
On Tuesday, it plunged to a low of 2.7930 a dollar, its weakest level since February 1994.
The market was likely to take a crack at the 2.80-mark, a low level not seen since the ringgit was officially floated in 1973, dealers and analysts said.

"The risk to the 2.80-level and beyond remains intact as the regionals are still vulnerable," said Ishak Ismail, markets analyst at research firm I.D.E.A. "The focus on rupiah today gave the ringgit some breathing space."
The ringgit, like other Southeast Asian currencies, has been hit by speculative attacks over the past month, losing nearly 12 percent of its value.
Analysts said they expected offshore funds to mount a fresh assault on the ringgit once they finished locking in profits.
"I think it will be very soon," said Derrick Lee, an analyst at market research firm Technical Data.
"After 2.80, I have no idea where the ringgit could go because it was never traded above that level before," he said.
Analysts said the fact that the ringgit has limited its gains to the 2.76/2.77 level also indicates that the downside pressure may not be over.
"Speculators may be enticed by the prospect of what lies beyond 2.80," said an analyst with a research firm in Singapore.
Worries about the Malaysian economy, weak regional currencies and the dollar's strength worldwide would continue to pressure the ringgit, analysts said.
"When all these factors combined, they become a poison cocktail," said Lee of Technical Data.
Analysts said a move beyond the 2.80-mark would put Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, in a very difficult position.
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim reiterated on Tuesday that the central bank will not intervene to defend the ringgit.
"We will look at the strength of the market and the...ringgit based on the strength of the economy. The question of intervention does not arise," he told reporters.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad had said on Friday that he was happy with the ringgit's level, triggering a sharp selldown in the currency.
Offshore dealers have been testing how far Bank Negara will tolerate the fall of the beleaguered currency.
Analysts said the central bank's absence and the fact that exporters had already sold off most of their dollar positions, were the main reasons for the lack of resistance to the fall.
